name: Question 15
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/928fb72015b78436f95895799c2846d1a0b34242b7216d31a6ed6bdda46728a1.png)

Evaluate the double integral ${∬}_{D}\frac{6x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A,$ where the region $D$ is shown above.
worked_solution:
We need to change the coordinate system from Cartesian coordinates to polar coordinates. To do this, we will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $4$ centered at $(0,0).$ 

Cartesian and polar coordinates are connected by the following equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's now write our curves in polar coordinates.

- For ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ we obtain $r=4.$

- For $x=2\sqrt{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =2\sqrt{2} \\ r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & =2\sqrt{2} \\ r & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\ r & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's find the limits for the parameter $\theta .$ Our curves intersect at the point $(2\sqrt{2},2\sqrt{2}).$ So, the entire region $D$ lies between the polar lines $\theta =0$ and $\theta =\frac{\pi }{4},$ as depicted below.  

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14056707/assets/375e270ce444d9f62b50f9a25abfae781113fdad895833d693061ffffe93f5d3.png)

As a result, the region can be expressed in polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$ as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta \le r\le 4,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{6x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{6r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,r\,\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{4}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {\int }_{2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{4}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta [r]_{2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }^{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}6\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (4-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}(24\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta -12\sqrt{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =[24\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta -12\sqrt{2}\,\theta ]_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =[(24\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-12\sqrt{2}(\frac{\pi }{4}))-0] \\  & =12\sqrt{2}-3\pi \sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
